citation: Kurz & Allison. Chicago In Early Days, 1779-1857. Chicago: Kurz & Allison, 76 & 78 Wabash Avenue, 1893. Chromolithograph, fifteen numbered vignettes with printed key.
author: Kurz & Allison
repository: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division; copy held in this repo at chicago/reference/photos/
locator: panel 1 (Old Fort Dearborn, erected 1803); panel 5 (Fort Dearborn as rebuilt 1835); panel 8 (Chicago in 1830 - From the Lake); panel 9 (Wolf Point in 1830); panel 11 (The Green Tree Hotel); panel 12 (The Old Kinzie Mansion, built 1832); panel 14 (The Sauganash Hotel). Four of those seven are committed in this project as crops and are joined to the sheet by measurement, not by recognition - panels 12, 1, 5 and 8, in tools/measure_plate_join.py, which re-measures all four on every commit.
note:
Fifteen retrospective vignettes of early Chicago with a printed key giving names, build dates and populations. Panel 14, 'The Sauganash Hotel. Built in 1831', shows a two-story clapboard block with an attached single-story log wing and NO full-width gallery — the composition follows the F. Braunhold engraving in Andreas (1884) closely enough that it is probably derived from it rather than an independent witness. Panel 5, 'Fort Dearborn as rebuilt 1835', is the most directly scene-relevant image in the sheet: picket palisade, a galleried barracks range, a blockhouse. Its own dating is unreliable — it puts the Kinzie Mansion at 1832, contradicting every documentary source.

PANEL 12 IS THE 'KINZIE-VIEW PLATE', AND THIS RECORD ALREADY HELD IT (T-0055). The plate the garden-fence layer has been citing by committed path since it was written — data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_1.png, 391 x 287 px, sha256 f796f89dbdc23a9a592bd722e9ddb0a55265efdbb55835a74fb0859fb17f6543, described in that directory's README as "the Kinzie mansion group (plate '12')" — is panel 12 of THIS sheet. It is a crop of it, and the project has held the whole sheet as a source since before the fence layer existed. So data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json's long-standing finding, 'this project holds NO source record for the Kinzie-view plate', was wrong in its conclusion while right about the symptom: the record was here and nothing joined it.

HOW THE JOIN WAS PROVED, rather than recognised. Three things agree and any one of them alone would be an eyeball. (a) The panel's own printed numeral: '12.' sits in the upper-left corner of p6_1 and in the upper-left corner of the sheet's lower-left vignette. (b) The printed key at the foot of the sheet, transcribed from the committed copy: "No. 12.  The Old Kinzie Mansion, built 1832.  Population 310." — the same 1832 build date this record's note already flags as unreliable, and the line immediately below "No. 11.  The Green Tree Hotel, cor. West Lake and Canal St.  Built in 1833.", whose panel is the set's OTHER numbered plate, p6_0, carrying '11.' in its own upper-right corner. (c) A normalised cross-correlation of p6_1 against the sheet (chicago/reference/photos/IMG_5382.png, 2048 x 1624): the best match over a scale sweep is 0.797 at 0.88x, at sheet pixels (94,1164)-(438,1416) — the lower-left vignette — against a best of 0.341 anywhere in the bird's-eye panel used as a control. The crop is the panel, at 88 % of the committed sheet's scale.

WHAT THAT CHANGES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. The garden fence's evidence is not one grade stronger for being identified: this is still panel 12 of a chromolithograph published fifty-eight years after the scene date, it is still tier 5, and it still may never drive a coordinate. What changes is that the citation is now a source_id with a date, a publisher, an expired copyright and a holding institution instead of a path into an asset directory, and that the reader who wants to check the fence can reach the Library of Congress scan rather than a 391-px crop. Note the direction of the rights news: the fence layer had been reading a plate it recorded as unheld and therefore un-cleared, and the plate is public domain.

THREE MORE PANELS JOINED, AND ONE OF THEM IS NOT WHAT ITS README SAID (T-1107). T-0055 proved panel 12 and deliberately left the fort crops unconfirmed, because its scope was the Kinzie plate and nothing else had been measured. T-1107 measured them, by the same method, now committed as tools/measure_plate_join.py so the next crop needs no fresh improvisation:
  data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p4_0.png = PANEL 1, "No. 1.  Old Fort Dearborn.  Erected 1803." - numeral '1.' in the crop's own upper-left corner and in the sheet's top-left vignette; ncc 0.896 at 0.295x, sheet pixels (99,78)-(553,331), against 0.400 anywhere in the control panel.
  p3_1.png = PANEL 5, "No. 5.  Fort Dearborn, as re[built] ... 1835.  Population 3,265." - numeral '5.' in the crop and in the sheet's top-right vignette; ncc 0.812 at 0.425x, sheet pixels (1486,77)-(1945,323), against 0.337.
  p4_1.png = PANEL 8, "No. 8.  Chicago in 1830 - From the Lake.  Population 96." - ncc 0.863 at 0.735x, sheet pixels (533,342)-(1511,831), against 0.325. This crop carries NO numeral: it is taken inside the frame of the sheet's centre vignette, whose number is printed OUTSIDE its top-left corner at sheet (572,304), where this sheet numbers its two largest panels.

PANEL 8 IS THE CORRECTION WORTH READING. The 2026-08-11 README described p4_0 and p4_1 as two views of "Fort Dearborn from across the river" and data/enclosures/fort_dearborn_apron.json called them "the two Fort Dearborn plates". They are two different subjects on one sheet: p4_0 is the post of 1803 and p4_1 is the TOWN of 1830, population 96, in which the fort is one building among many - five years before the scene date and before the rebuilt walls of panel 5. Nothing measured off p4_1 is retracted; tools/measure_fort_ways_plate.py and tools/generate_fort_trees.py ask it what the picture draws, and being named does not change the picture. What changes is the date a reader should attach to the answer.

The control figure reproduces T-0055's to a thousandth (0.342 here against the 0.341 it recorded) on the same crop, which is the calibration that lets the other three be believed.

All three are higher-resolution than the committed whole-sheet photograph - they match it at 0.295x, 0.425x and 0.735x of their own pixels - so the crops, not the sheet, are the copy to read a detail off.
rights_note: The sheet carries its own copyright line at the foot, read off the committed copy verbatim: "Copyrighted 1893 by Kurz & Allison, 76 & 78 Wabash Avenue, Chicago, Ills." A US copyright first secured in 1893 has expired, which is why this record is public_domain rather than check_required, and it is the only plate in this project's pictorial set whose rights are settled ON THE OBJECT rather than by inference. The Library of Congress copy at the url carries no restriction of its own.
what_it_supplies: panel 1: Old Fort Dearborn of 1803 from across the river - the palisade under a ruled cap line, the barracks ranges, the blockhouses and the bare trodden ground outside the walls that data/enclosures/fort_dearborn_apron.json is built on

panel 8: the town from the lake in 1830, population 96 - the low far bank, a lodge and bark canoes on the shore, and trees round the buildings on both banks; a scene-adjacent TOWN view, five years early, not a second view of the fort
panel 12: the long low Kinzie house with a full-width piazza on its front, a red roof, and outbuildings up the rise behind it
panel 12: a row of four Lombardy poplars standing between the house and the river — the count and rhythm tools/generate_planted_rows.py measures across seven plates
panel 12: PICKET-FENCED garden plots at the house — close-set vertical pales, the treatment data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json deals to the town's house lots
panel 12: the fenced green between house and water that Wau-Bun describes in words, drawn
panel 11: the Green Tree Hotel as a two-storey clapboard block with end chimneys and even sash, with ship masts behind it
panel 5: Fort Dearborn as rebuilt 1835 — picket palisade, galleried barracks range, blockhouse
panel 14: the Sauganash Hotel as a two-storey clapboard block with an attached single-storey log wing and no full-width gallery
the sheet's printed key, which names each panel and dates several of the buildings
what_it_does_not_supply: any coordinate, footprint outline or dimension — tier 5, and a perspective vignette cannot be asked for a metre
a date for anything it draws that can be relied on: its own key puts the Kinzie Mansion at 1832, which contradicts every documentary source this project holds
independent testimony for panel 14, which follows the F. Braunhold engraving in Andreas (1884) closely enough to be probably derived from it
any evidence that a garden fence stood on a lot in the town: panel 12 is the north bank, and the house it draws is excluded from the 1835 scene (data/exclusions.json, kinzie_house)
a height, a pale width or a bay for the fence it draws — every dimension on the fence layer is invented, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L129 says so
a Lombardy poplar anywhere in Chicago but this one group
a view of the 1835 fort in panel 8: that panel is dated 1830 by the sheet's own key and was mistaken for a fort plate for a month (T-1107)
